Bell’s palsy

Two 2024 evidence syntheses and several controlled trials generally report better short-term facial-function scores with laser-based treatments. Protocols and co-interventions vary, so a durable PBM-specific effect and one preferred treatment schedule remain uncertain.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Lin et al. 2024 meta-analysis (9 of 12 trials pooled; 597 adults overall), laser therapy versus control care: House–Brackmann mean difference −1.51 (95% CI −2.43 to −0.59); Sunnybrook +20.63 (95% CI 10.33 to 30.94); Facial Disability Index +17.91 (95% CI 5.60 to 30.22). These pool differing laser approaches and are not specific to one PBM protocol.

Wu et al. 2024 single-center RCT (84 randomized; 79 analyzed), laser acupuncture plus PBM versus a low-output device control: abnormal House–Brackmann grade at reported week 12, 11/42 versus 32/42 (OR 0.11; 95% CI 0.04–0.30; p<0.001). Sunnybrook score difference was +20.26 points (95% CI 14.69–25.83; p<0.001). The paper also reports 72 sessions over 24 weeks and day-180 assessments in Methods, so the follow-up timing is unclear.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term facial-function outcomes with PBM as an adjunct (Lin et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2024; Alayat et al. 2022)

Low for durable recovery and less-studied patient groups (Amiri and Fekrazad 2024; Wu et al. 2024)

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two 2024 evidence syntheses and several controlled trials generally report better short-term facial-function scores with laser-based treatments. Protocols and co-interventions vary, so a durable PBM-specific effect and one preferred treatment schedule remain uncertain.

Summary of the Evidence

Short-term facial-function outcomes generally favor laser-based treatment, but results come from varied disease stages, doses, comparators, and co-interventions. Reviews describe a similar positive direction while emphasizing that protocols and measures differ. The evidence does not establish one optimal PBM schedule or a durable effect.

Human and clinical evidence

A 2024 systematic review covered Bell’s-palsy PBM studies published from 1993 through 2022. It described improvements in facial function, pain, and muscle strength, while highlighting substantial variation in study designs, wavelengths, doses, and outcome measures (Amiri and Fekrazad 2024).

A separate 2024 meta-analysis identified 12 randomized studies with 597 adults and pooled nine. Its estimates favor laser therapy over control care on House–Brackmann facial-nerve grade, Sunnybrook facial function, and Facial Disability Index. The included approaches and comparators vary, so pooled laser estimates should not be read as an effect of one standardized PBM protocol (Lin et al. 2024).

A single-center, single-blind randomized study enrolled 84 adults with Bell’s palsy lasting more than eight weeks. It compared 808/905-nm laser acupuncture plus PBM with a low-output control using the same device. Facial-function and electrophysiological outcomes favored the active protocol, but this combined intervention cannot isolate PBM. The article reports follow-up as 12 weeks in Results, while its methods describe 72 sessions three times weekly and assessments at day 180; the timing is internally inconsistent (Wu et al. 2024).

A double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 60 people with subacute Bell’s palsy compared multiwave locked-system laser treatment with placebo and reported better facial-function outcomes over six weeks (Alayat et al. 2022). Other controlled reports and case series describe both favorable and unclear results. Two case reports involving broader peripheral facial palsy are related evidence, not direct Bell’s-palsy studies.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly models idiopathic Bell’s palsy in the indication records. Two rat facial-nerve-injury studies provide adjacent nerve-repair evidence but are not direct disease models.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study directly examines Bell’s palsy.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical records use near-infrared wavelengths around 808–905 nm, sometimes with 660-nm red visible light. Reported fluences commonly fall around 8–20 J/cm², but treatment sites, session lengths, schedules, disease stage, and added exercise or acupuncture vary. The 84-person chronic-palsy trial used an ASA Mphi multiwave laser for laser acupuncture plus PBM; its report does not support assuming the same effect from PBM alone. No head-to-head trial establishes a preferred device or dose.

Interpretation

Pooled facial-function scores and several controlled studies favor laser-based treatment in the short term. The evidence is less certain for durability and for separating PBM from laser acupuncture or other co-interventions. Larger blinded trials using a common protocol and consistent follow-up would clarify the clinical effect.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Recent pooled syntheses and controlled trials generally favor laser-based treatment on short-term facial-function scales (Lin et al. 2024; Amiri and Fekrazad 2024). However, pooled studies combine different laser methods and comparators, including laser acupuncture, and several trials are small or single-center. One chronic Bell’s-palsy RCT also reports inconsistent timing across its methods and results (Wu et al. 2024). Larger blinded trials with a shared protocol and longer follow-up would clarify PBM-specific benefit and durability.
